title: Chapter XXI

teacherSummary.text: Collins turns his attention elsewhere. Charlotte draws him away. The Bingley party leaves for London, and Caroline writes that Bingley will not return and hints he may marry Darcy's sister, Georgiana.

vocabulary.definition: To give up, the will, courage, or spirit
vocabulary.context: Jane’s temper was not desponding, and she was gradually led to hope, though the diffidence of affection sometimes overcame the hope, that Bingley would return to Netherfield and answer every wish of her heart.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “despond”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + pon (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I really do not think Georgiana Darcy has her equal for beauty, elegance, and accomplishments; and the affection she inspires in Louisa and myself, is heightened into something still more interesting, from the hope we dare to entertain of her being hereafter our sister.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inspire”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: With all these circumstances to favour an attachment and nothing to prevent it, am I wrong, my dearest Jane, in indulging the hope of an event which will secure the happiness of so many?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “indulge”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: As for the gentleman himself, his feelings were chiefly expressed, not by embarrassment or dejection, or by trying to avoid her, but by stiffness of manner and resentful silence.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dejection”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -tion (Latin -tio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: His accompanying them was a double advantage; she felt all the compliment it offered to herself, and it was most acceptable as an occasion of introducing him to her father and mother.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “introduce”: intro- (Latin intro, "inward") + duc (Latin ducere, "to lead"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Caroline is incapable of wilfully deceiving anyone; and all that I can hope in this case is, that she is deceived herself.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “deceive”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + ceive (Latin capere, "to take"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To go with or attend as a companion or associate
vocabulary.context: His accompanying them was a double advantage; she felt all the compliment it offered to herself, and it was most acceptable as an occasion of introducing him to her father and mother.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “accompany”: ac- (Latin ad, "to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To receive with a consenting mind (something offered)
vocabulary.context: “But, my dear sister, can I be happy, even supposing the best, in accepting a man whose sisters and friends are all wishing him to marry elsewhere?”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “accept”: ac- (Latin ad, "to") + cept (Latin capere, "to take"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of moving from one point to another
vocabulary.context: Bingley would be soon down again and soon dining at Longbourn, and the conclusion of all was the comfortable declaration that, though he had been invited only to a family dinner, she would take care to have two full courses.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “course”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Equal in wortir or value, force, power, effect, import, and the like
vocabulary.context: “You must decide for yourself,” said Elizabeth, “and if upon mature deliberation, you find that the misery of disobliging his two sisters is more than equivalent to the happiness of being his wife, I advise you by all means to refuse him.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “equivalent”: -ent (Latin -ens, "one who, doing"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: London's 'season' was the high point of social and marriage activity.

significance: Caroline's letter deceives Jane and begins her heartbreak.
discussionQuestions: Is Caroline's letter honest? What might her motives be?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXI,” how does Austen show consequences of refusal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXI develops the idea of consequences of refusal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and plot shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXI to complicate the reader's understanding of consequences of refusal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of consequences of refusal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of consequences of refusal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: The discussion of Mr. Collins’s offer was now nearly at an end, and Elizabeth had only to suffer from the uncomfortable feelings necessarily attending it, and occasionally from some peevish allusion of her mother. As for the gentleman himself, his feelings were chiefly expressed, not by embarrassment or dejection, or by trying to avoid her, but by stiffness of manner and resentful silence. He scarcely ever spoke to her, and the assiduous attentions which he had been so sensible of himself, were transferred for the rest of the day to Miss Lucas, whose civility in listening to him, was a seasonable relief to them all, and especially to her friend.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XXI”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Is Caroline's letter honest? What might her motives be? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are desponding, inspires, indulging, dejection, introducing. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Jane’s temper was not desponding, and she was gradually led to hope, though the diffidence of affection sometimes overcame the hope, that Bingley would return to Netherfield and answer every wish of her heart.” Webster's says: To give up, the will, courage, or spirit. Now the word history: “despond”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + pon (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “inspire”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “indulge”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. London's 'season' was the high point of social and marriage activity. Why does this chapter matter? Caroline's letter deceives Jane and begins her heartbreak. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to consequences of refusal.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Plot, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

As for the gentleman himself, his feelings were chiefly expressed, not by embarrassment or dejection, or by trying to avoid her, but by stiffness of manner and resentful silence. He scarcely ever spoke to her, and the assiduous attentions which he had been so sensible of himself, were transferred for the rest of the day to Miss Lucas, whose civility in listening to him, was a seasonable relief to them all, and especially to her friend.

Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXI,” how does Austen show consequences of refusal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about consequences of refusal, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
